analysis.one_liner: Makes it harder for workers to form and keep a union, and restricts union dues and strikes.
analysis.headline: The Employee Rights Act never got a House vote: introduced with 29 cosponsors, all Republican, it sat in the Education and the Workforce Committee until the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal labor law in several ways. It would require a secret ballot election run by the government before workers get a union, count everyone in the workplace rather than just those who vote, require a new election every three years to keep an existing union, and impose a 40-day waiting period before any election. It would also require a majority of all affected employees to approve any strike, let nonmembers vote on union contracts and strikes, and block unions from spending dues on politics unless each worker signs a written yearly permission.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers gain the most: a longer election window gives them time to campaign against a union, the 'majority of all employees' standard makes winning an election harder, and mandatory three-year recertification elections threaten every existing union with removal. Workers who do not want a union, or who object to dues funding political activity, would gain new tools to end or limit representation. Workers who strike would be limited by a new requirement that a majority of all affected employees vote to approve a strike.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every union election to be a secret ballot run by the National Labor Relations Board, and defines 'majority' as a majority of all employees in the unit, not just those who vote, so workers who stay home count against the union [S2].
Requires a new secret ballot election every three years, at shared employer-union cost, to decide whether an existing union stays certified; if a majority votes no, certification is withdrawn [S3].

Bars any election within 40 days of a petition and requires hearings and review of all pre-election appeals before an election can be held, extending the process during which an employer can campaign against the union [S2, S3].

Prohibits a strike unless a majority of all affected employees consent by secret ballot, with the election run by a neutral private organization and paid for by the union; if the employer has made an offer, employees must vote on that offer before any strike vote [S3].

Bars unions from spending any employee's dues for purposes not directly related to bargaining unless that employee signs a written authorization, which expires after one year with no automatic renewal [S3].
Gives every employee in a bargaining unit, whether or not a union member, the right to vote on ratifying contracts and on going on strike [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Labor unions would lose members, dues, and political spending: three-year recertification votes put every certified union at risk, annual written permission requirements would cut voluntary dues and end dues-based political contributions, and the strike-approval rules would sharply limit unions' main bargaining tool. Workers who rely on unions would face weaker representation and less bargaining power; many employers' labor costs would fall as unions shrink.

drawbacks.text: The three-year recertification requirement, combined with counting non-voters against the union, makes it much harder to keep any union in place, including ones workers chose; the 40-day waiting period before an election gives employers more time to campaign against organizing [S3].

Requiring a secret ballot majority of all affected employees before any strike would make strikes nearly impossible to start, removing a key source of bargaining power for workers negotiating wages and conditions [S3].

Ending dues spending on any non-bargaining purpose without annual written permission, including on political activity, would sharply reduce union advocacy on legislation affecting their members' workplaces [S3].

Criminal penalties of up to 10 years and $100,000 for union-related force or threats are already largely covered by existing extortion and labor law, and supporters of unions argue the provision is aimed at painting organizing as violent [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill packages real protections for individual workers — secret ballots, freedom from coerced dues, criminal penalties for violence — with structural changes that would make unions substantially harder to win and keep. The individual protections mostly codify rights that already exist in some form, while the recertification, election-timing, strike-vote, and dues provisions would shift bargaining power toward employers. On the whole, the cost to collective bargaining outweighs the added individual safeguards.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Scott introduced the Employee Rights Act on August 5, 2011, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S1, S5].
Twenty-nine other House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].
The committee held no markup and the House never voted on the bill; the record shows no action after the referral [S5].
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, and the bill expired without a vote [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Labor unions and the workers they represent kept the existing organizing rules, since no election ever took place on the bill; employers gained nothing, but also lost nothing, because the status quo held.

sides.party_line_note: All 30 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never reached a roll call.

industries.note: Three-year recertification elections, a harder election standard, strike-approval votes, and annual written permission for dues would cut union membership, dues, and bargaining power. Unions' interest runs with the workers they represent, though their dues and political spending are the direct targets.

A 40-day minimum election window gives employers more time to campaign against organizing, the majority-of-all-employees standard makes unions harder to win and keep, and the strike rules limit workers' ability to withhold labor. The gain comes at the cost of workers' collective bargaining.

industries.industry: Anti-union advocacy groups and law firms
industries.note: Recertification elections and expanded decertification mechanics would create recurring election campaigns and legal work built around removing unions.
